decisions.quote: We were not able to reproduce the misattribution effects of anxiety-related arousal on ERN/Ne that have been found by Inzlicht and Al-Khindi (2012). Even in a subsample of the misattribution group with below-average state-anxiety, the ERN/Ne effect of the original study could not be replicated.
decisions.location: Conclusion, line 79 (see also Abstract, line 8; Discussion, lines 70-73)
decisions.reason: The central finding under test—and the sole focus of both the original and replication titles, the power calculation (line 27), and the primary aim statement (lines 8, 24)—is the modulation of the ERN/Ne by placebo-induced misattribution of state-anxiety following errors. In the original study, the absence of a group difference in behavioral performance served only in combination with the significant ERN/Ne reduction to establish a dissociation between ERN/Ne and cognitive performance (lines 20, 69). In this replication, the misattribution manipulation produced no group difference on state-anxiety (manipulation check), no group effect or interaction on ERN/Ne (full sample or low-anxiety subgroup), and no moderation of the dERN/Ne–error correlation (which was significant in both groups, contrary to the original). Even for the null performance comparison, the authors report that the equality-of-effect-size Bayes factor showed 'no clear replication success of the null results for the performance measures' (line 70) and conclude that the original dissociation between performance and ERN/Ne was not supported (line 73). Under the codebook rules to code the central finding the replication was designed to test and to code 'failed' when the title-focused effect fails to replicate regardless of ancillary control/specificity checks, the outcome is 'failed'.
